question: What does the abbreviation "MEA" stand for on an IFR en-route chart?

options.text: Minimum En-route Altitude
Maximum En-route Altitude
Minimum Enroute Approach
Mean En-route Altitude

explanation: MEA is the lowest published altitude between two fixes that meets obstacle clearance requirements and ensures acceptable navigation signal coverage for the route segment.

question: What is the primary difference between flying under IFR and flying under VFR?

options.text: IFR flights may only be conducted at night
IFR flight is conducted with reference to flight instruments and an ATC clearance, rather than primarily by visual reference to the ground and horizon
VFR flights may never be flown above 10,000 ft
IFR flights never require an ATC clearance

explanation: IFR is a set of rules for flying with reference to instruments, under an ATC clearance and separation service, used when visual reference cannot be relied upon or is not sufficient — not a rule about time of day.

question: What does "MOCA" (Minimum Obstruction Clearance Altitude) define on a route segment?

options.text: The lowest altitude guaranteeing obstacle clearance on that segment, though reliable navigation signal coverage may only be assured within a limited distance of a facility
The minimum altitude at which an aircraft may be operated in cruise flight anywhere
The maximum obstacle height permitted directly under an airway
The minimum altitude required for overwater flight

explanation: MOCA guarantees obstacle clearance for the whole segment, but away from the navigation facility, signal reception may not be assured — unlike MEA, which also guarantees signal coverage throughout.

question: A "standard rate" (Rate 1) turn used in instrument flying is a turn at approximately what rate?

options.text: 1 degree per second
2 degrees per second
3 degrees per second
6 degrees per second

explanation: A standard rate turn is 3 degrees per second, completing a 360-degree turn in 2 minutes. It is the reference turn rate instrument pilots use, and what a turn coordinator is calibrated to show.

question: What characterises RVSM (Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum) airspace?

options.text: The vertical separation minimum between eligible aircraft is reduced from 2,000 ft to 1,000 ft within a defined band of flight levels
It is airspace reserved exclusively for VFR traffic
It refers to a reduced-visibility segment on an approach chart
It reduces the horizontal separation minima between departures only

explanation: RVSM airspace, typically between FL290 and FL410, allows 1,000 ft vertical separation instead of the usual 2,000 ft above FL290, increasing capacity, but requires the aircraft and its altimetry system to meet defined performance standards.

question: What does a published Minimum Sector Altitude (MSA) on an approach chart guarantee?

options.text: Obstacle clearance within a specified radius of a facility, for emergency use only — not intended for routine navigation
The lowest altitude at which the aircraft may cruise anywhere in the country
The minimum altitude required for VFR flight in that area
The altitude to fly after a missed approach, replacing the published procedure

explanation: MSA provides at least the required obstacle clearance within a defined radius (commonly 25 NM) of a facility or fix, intended as an emergency reference — routine descent still follows the published procedure, not the MSA.

question: Which statement best describes Class A airspace?

options.text: Airspace open to VFR flights only
Airspace where IFR flight is mandatory and VFR flight is not permitted, typically found at higher altitudes
Uncontrolled airspace with no ATC service
Airspace reserved exclusively for military operations

explanation: Class A airspace requires all flights to operate under IFR and be subject to ATC clearance and separation; VFR flight is not permitted in it.

question: What is the main purpose of filing an IFR flight plan before departure?

options.text: It is only ever required for international flights
It gives ATC the aircraft's intended route, altitude, speed and other details so separation and flight-following services can be provided throughout the flight
It replaces the need for a pre-flight weather briefing
It is used only to reserve a parking stand at the destination

explanation: The flight plan is the basis ATC uses to provide clearances, separation and search-and-rescue alerting; a weather briefing is a separate, still-necessary part of flight preparation.
